native_result.query: How does incarceration affect the wealth of black individuals based on their income levels?
native_result.HypoA: The negative impact of incarceration on wealth for black individuals may be less for the high-income group than those at lower wealth ranges.
native_result.HypoB: Among black NLSY79 respondents, ever having been jailed (1985-1994) is associated with sharply lower wealth by 1996 at every baseline (1985) wealth/income position, but the form of the association varies across the distribution: in the lowest baseline-wealth tercile (<= $0 in 1985; jailed n=76 vs never n=1,240) floor effects compress median differences (both $0), and the penalty appears as a much lower probability of accumulating any positive wealth by 1996 (22% vs 45%; mean gap -$17,181); in the middle tercile ($0-$3,830; n=39 vs 654), starting wealth is identical (median $1,400) yet jailed respondents' median wealth falls to $0 by 1996 vs $7,450 for never-jailed (mean gap -$29,393; DiD-style mean-change gap 1985->1996 of -$29,391); and in the highest tercile (>$3,830; n=44 vs 960), jailed respondents' median wealth does not grow at all, falling from $11,150 (1985) to $4,700 (1996) while never-jailed peers rise from $11,900 to $26,750 (median gap -$22,050; DiD mean-change gap -$59,008). The incarceration-wealth association among black individuals is therefore weakest in absolute wealth terms at the bottom (nothing-to-lose floor effect) and strongest in the middle and upper baseline-wealth strata, where it manifests as stagnant or negative wealth growth and a roughly halved probability of holding positive wealth. No income variable exists in the data, so 'income levels' are proxied by 1985 composite wealth terciles. These are observational associations conditional on baseline wealth, not causal estimates: jailing status spans 1985-1994 (the 1990 comparison is contemporaneous with the window, not a clean pre/post), composite wealth construction/units are undocumented, ~30-41% of wealth values are <=0 (floor effects), treated cells are small (39-76 per tercile), sex is the only covariate (jailed black respondents are overwhelmingly male: 143/1,465 men vs 16/1,548 women; the negative association holds in both sexes), and the processed file's complete absence of missing values precludes assessing panel attrition.
native_result.WorkflowB: 1) Loaded data/nls_incarceration_processed.csv (12,013 rows; verified race values white/black/'hipanic' [typo of hispanic, reported as observed], ever_jailed clean 0/1, zero missingness; wealth composites heavily right-skewed and zero-inflated with negative values, no top-coding). 2) Because the dataset has no income variable, proxied 'income levels' with baseline (1985) composite wealth, restricted to black respondents (n=3,013, 159 ever-jailed). 3) Stratified black respondents into 1985-wealth terciles (primary) and compared ever-jailed vs never-jailed within each stratum on 1990 and 1996 wealth levels (medians primary, means secondary, n per cell reported) and on within-stratum change 1985->1990 and 1985->1996 (DiD-style: jailed-group change minus never-jailed-group change); 1990 labeled contemporaneous-with-window, 1996 given equal weight as the post-window outcome. 4) Sensitivity: winsorization at 99th percentile, positive-wealth indicator, quartile stratification restricted to strata with jailed n>=30 (Q2 skipped, n=7). 5) Sex-stratified sanity check within the black subsample plus sex-demeaned pooled comparison. 6) Secondary white reference contrast with identical tercile design. Scripts: analysis/nls_incarceration_analysis.py, analysis/did_fix_and_quartiles.py; full printed output in analysis/analysis_output.txt.
